title: Clinical records: law & good practice
blurb: What goes in a dental record, how to write and correct entries, how long records are kept, and who can see them.
question: After a filling you realise you typed the local anaesthetic batch number into the wrong patient's notes. The dentist has gone to lunch. How do you put it right, and what makes a record entry good enough to rely on if there is ever a complaint?

teach.body: A dental record is a legal document. It lets the next clinician continue care safely, shows what the patient was told and agreed to, and is the main evidence if there's a complaint, a claim or a GDC investigation. GDC Principle 4 says you must make and keep contemporaneous, complete and accurate records. As the nurse you often write or type entries for the dentist, so the quality of the record is partly your responsibility. If it isn't written down, it is very hard to prove it happened.

letters.sub: Written at the time, or as soon as possible after
Readable by anyone; standard abbreviations only
Only what actually happened, nothing left out
The author can be identified (or logged in as themselves)

head: Part
Includes
rows: Name, date of birth, address, contacts, GP
Updated and checked at each course of treatment
Charting, BPE, soft tissues, radiographs and their reports
Options, risks, costs and the patient's decision
What was done, materials, LA type, dose and batch
Letters, refusals, missed or cancelled appointments

teach.body: Never write that a colleague did something you didn't witness, and never fill in an entry to make the notes 'look complete'. An entry should say what was done, what was advised and what is planned next, so a different clinician can pick up safely. Refusals count too: if a patient declines a radiograph, record that the reasons and consequences were explained and the decision respected. Use only widely understood abbreviations. If you can't understand an entry, ask the person who wrote it rather than guessing.

steps.label: Don't delete or hide it
steps.sub: No correction fluid, scribbling or overwriting

steps.label: Mark the error
steps.sub: Single line through (paper) or amend the entry (software)

steps.label: Sign, date and time it
steps.sub: Electronic systems keep an audit trail

teach.caption: The original must stay readable. A correction that's visible and explained shows honesty; a hidden one looks like falsification.

teach.caption: From the NHS Records Management Code. Follow your practice policy for how the 11-year rule and the children's rule combine.

teach.body: Patients have a legal right to see their records under UK GDPR (a subject access request), normally answered within one month and usually free. Records of patients who have died can be requested by their personal representative under the Access to Health Records Act 1990. Keep paper records locked away and electronic records password protected and backed up. Never share your login, and always log in as yourself, because the system records who wrote each entry. Destroy records securely once the retention period ends.

teach.text: 'Contemporaneous' doesn't mean 'some time this week'. Write the record during or straight after the appointment. A note written days later, from memory, is less reliable and harder to defend.

items: Records are legal documents: contemporaneous, legible, accurate and complete, signed and dated, secure.
Record only what actually happened, including advice, plans and refusals.
Correct errors openly: line through or amend, add the correct entry, give the reason, sign and date.
Keep dental records 11 years; children's generally to age 25 (26 if 17 when treatment ended), per local policy.
Patients can see their records: respond within one month.

summary: You can now explain why dental records matter, list what they contain, write entries that are contemporaneous, legible, accurate, signed and secure, correct a mistake properly, and state how long records are kept and who can see them.

A.q: You realise you recorded treatment in the wrong patient's notes. What is the correct action?
options: Delete the entry and retype it in the right notes
Amend it, showing the change and reason
Leave it, as the dentist will notice
Cover it with correction fluid
A.why: Corrections must be visible and explained: amend the entry, record the reason and sign and date it, then add the entry to the right record.

whyNot.0: Deleting removes the audit trail and can look like falsification.
whyNot.2: An error in a record must be corrected promptly, not left for someone else.
whyNot.3: The original entry must remain readable.

A.q: What does 'contemporaneous' mean when applied to clinical records?
options: Typed rather than handwritten
Checked by a second person
Written at the time or soon after
Kept for the full retention period
A.why: Contemporaneous records are made at the time of the event or as soon as possible afterwards.

whyNot.0: Records can be paper or electronic; timing is what matters.
whyNot.1: Checking is good practice but isn't what the word means.
whyNot.3: That describes retention, not contemporaneous recording.

A.q: For how long should adult dental care records normally be kept?
options: 11 years
6 years
15 years
25 years
A.why: Dental care records are kept for 11 years. This changed from 15 years in May 2023.

whyNot.1: Six years is not the dental records retention period.
whyNot.2: 15 years was the old period, replaced in May 2023.
whyNot.3: 25 relates to children's records (until the 25th birthday), not years for adults.

B.q: A colleague asks you to record that she completed a task you didn't witness. Which principle applies?
options: Records should be completed quickly
Records must reflect what actually happened
Senior staff can authorise entries for others
It is fine if the task was routine
B.why: Records must be accurate and reflect what actually happened. Only record what you did or saw.

whyNot.2: Seniority doesn't make an inaccurate entry acceptable.
whyNot.3: Routine or not, you can't record what you didn't witness.

B.q: A patient will see a different dentist next time. Which entry best supports continuity of care?
options: The appointment length and room
A note that the patient was pleasant and chatty
The fee charged for the visit
What was done, advised and planned next
B.why: A good entry tells the next clinician what was done, what advice was given and what happens next.

whyNot.0: Room and length don't help the next clinician treat safely.
whyNot.1: Personal comments are unhelpful and may be unprofessional.
whyNot.2: Fees belong in financial records, not the clinical plan for next time.

B.q: A patient's notes contain an abbreviation nobody recognises. What is the safest action?
options: Ask the author what it means
Work it out from the context
Ignore it and carry on
Delete it from the notes
B.why: Misread abbreviations can cause errors. Check with the person who wrote it before relying on it.

whyNot.1: A wrong guess could lead to the wrong treatment.
whyNot.2: Ignoring it may mean missing something important.
whyNot.3: You must never delete another clinician's entry.

C.q: A patient declines a radiograph the dentist recommends. What should be recorded?
options: Nothing, as no treatment was given
Only that the radiograph wasn't taken
The explanation given and their decision
A note that the patient was being difficult
C.why: Recording the discussion, the consequences explained and the patient's decision shows the refusal was informed.

whyNot.0: Refusals are part of the record and must be documented.
whyNot.1: Without the discussion, the note doesn't show the decision was informed.
whyNot.3: Judgemental comments are unprofessional and don't belong in records.

C.q: A child finished treatment at age 12. Under the NHS code, children's records are generally kept until when?
options: Their 18th birthday
Their 21st birthday
Five years after treatment
Their 25th birthday
C.why: Children's records are generally kept until the 25th birthday (26th if they were 17 when treatment ended). Follow local policy for how this combines with the 11-year rule.

whyNot.0: 18 is too early; claims can be brought for some years after adulthood.
whyNot.2: Five years is far too short for any dental record.

C.q: Which is NOT a feature of a good clinical record?
options: Written at the time of treatment
Signed and dated by the author
Uses personal shorthand to save time
Stored securely, with access controlled
C.why: Personal shorthand can be misread by others. Only widely understood abbreviations should be used.

reteach.title: Write it for a stranger
reteach.question: Imagine a dentist you've never met opens these notes in three years' time, with no one to ask. Could they work out exactly what happened?

blocks.body: Every entry should make sense to a stranger: a locum next week, a specialist after referral, or a GDC caseworker years later. They need to know who wrote it, when, what was found, what was done (with materials and batch numbers), what the patient was told and agreed, and what happens next. Vague notes, private shorthand or a missing date leave them guessing, and guesses in healthcare cause harm.

blocks.text: Changing a record after a complaint, without showing the change, is one of the quickest ways to lose your registration. Corrections must always be visible, dated and explained.

explain.body: Record only what happened, at the time. Include what was done, advised and planned, plus refusals. Use standard abbreviations.

test.q: Why should abbreviations be used carefully in clinical records?
options: They take longer to type than full words
Others relying on the record may misread them
Patients are not allowed to see them
They are banned under GDC record-keeping guidance
test.why: A misread abbreviation can lead to the wrong treatment. Use only widely understood ones.

whyNot.0: Abbreviations are usually quicker, which is why they're tempting.
whyNot.2: Patients can see their whole record, abbreviations included.
whyNot.3: The GDC doesn't ban abbreviations; it expects clear, accurate records.

explain.body: Never delete, overwrite or use correction fluid. Mark the error, add the correct entry, give the reason, then sign, date and time it.

test.q: On a paper record, how should an incorrect entry be corrected?
options: Scribble over it so it can't be read
Tear out the page and rewrite it
Use correction fluid neatly, then initial it
Single line through it, signed and dated
test.why: A single line keeps the original readable. Add the correction and reason, signed and dated.

whyNot.1: Removing pages destroys part of a legal document.
whyNot.2: Correction fluid hides the original entry.

explain.body: Dental care records: 11 years (since May 2023). Children's records: generally until the 25th birthday, or 26th if 17 when treatment ended. Follow local policy.

test.q: What was the dental records retention period changed to in May 2023?
options: 7 years
10 years
11 years
15 years
test.why: It changed from 15 years to 11 years, based on the Limitation Act 1980.

whyNot.0: Seven years is not the dental standard.
whyNot.1: Ten years is close but not the figure.

explain.body: Patients can request their records (one month, usually free). Records must be locked or password protected; log in only as yourself.

test.q: A colleague asks to use your login because hers has expired. What should you do?
options: Let her, as long as you're present
Decline and help her get access reset
Let her, but log out afterwards
Give her your password for today only
test.why: Entries must be attributable to the person who made them. Never share your login.

whyNot.0: Entries would still appear as yours.
whyNot.2: Logging out afterwards doesn't fix entries made under your name.
whyNot.3: Sharing passwords breaks security and accountability.
